title: 07. Messaging & Event-Driven Architecture: Apache Kafka

objectives: Why is Kafka called a "log" rather than a "queue," and what does that distinction imply?
How does partitioning work, and why is the partition count the parallelism ceiling?
What is the ISR (In-Sync Replicas), and how does it interact with the producer's `acks` setting?

sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** Apache Kafka is a distributed, partitioned, replicated, append-only commit log where producers write messages to topics, brokers store them durably in partitions ordered by offset, and consumer groups read them in parallel at their own pace — designed for millions of messages per second with multi-day retention and replay.

Kafka is not a queue in the traditional sense — it is a distributed log. The distinction matters: a queue (RabbitMQ, SQS) removes a message after a consumer acks, so the message has a single lifecycle; a log retains messages for a configurable period (days to weeks), so multiple independent consumers can read the same message at different times, replay it from the beginning, or skip ahead. This single design choice — durable retention with offset-based reads — is what makes Kafka the backbone of the modern data infrastructure at LinkedIn (who built it), Netflix, Uber, Instagram, Twitter, and most Fortune 500 companies. LinkedIn processes 7 trillion messages per day through Kafka; Netflix's entire event pipeline (plays, pauses, recommendations, billing) flows through it; Uber's trip, location, and pricing events stream through it; Instagram's notification and feed fan-out runs on it. Kafka's design is the answer to one question: how do you build a system that handles millions of messages per second, durably, with multiple independent consumers, and replay capability, using commodity hardware?

The core abstractions are topics, partitions, offsets, consumer groups, and replicas. A **topic** is a named stream — `user_events`, `orders`, `logs` — analogous to a queue name but with multi-consumer semantics. A topic is split into **partitions** (typically 6 to 100s), each an ordered, append-only log stored on disk as a sequence of segments. Each message in a partition has an **offset** (a monotonically increasing integer, 0, 1, 2, ...), and consumers track their position by committing offsets — this is how Kafka achieves at-least-once delivery without per-message ack. A **consumer group** is a set of consumers that share a topic: each partition is assigned to exactly one consumer in the group, so the group reads the topic in parallel; if a consumer dies, the partition is reassigned to a surviving consumer (rebalance). Different consumer groups read independently — one group might be 5 minutes behind, another 5 hours behind, and Kafka does not care. **Replication**: each partition has a leader replica and N follower replicas (typically 3); producers write to the leader, followers replicate; the **ISR (In-Sync Replicas)** is the set of followers caught up with the leader; if the leader dies, an ISR follower is elected the new leader. The replication factor (typically 3) and the producer's `acks` setting (`acks=0` fire-and-forget, `acks=1` leader-only, `acks=all` all ISR) determine the durability guarantee.

The throughput model is what makes Kafka unique. Each partition is a single file on disk, written sequentially and read sequentially — the optimal access pattern for spinning disks and SSDs alike, sustaining 100s of MB/sec per partition. Producers batch messages (default 16KB or 5ms, whichever comes first) before sending, amortizing network and disk overhead. The broker writes the batch to the OS page cache with a single `sendfile` syscall and calls `fsync` periodically (not per message), so writes are as fast as the OS can buffer them — typically 100k–1M messages/sec per broker, and millions per cluster. Reads are served from the page cache when possible (hot data), avoiding disk I/O entirely. The combination — sequential I/O, batching, page cache, zero-copy `sendfile` — is why Kafka sustains 7 trillion messages/day at LinkedIn while RabbitMQ and SQS top out at ~50k/sec per node. The trade-off is that Kafka is a log, not a queue: no per-message priorities, no per-message delays (must be emulated with delay topics), no individual ack (replaced by offset commits), and consumer logic must handle redelivery (at-least-once) by being idempotent.

Real-world deployments illustrate the patterns. **LinkedIn** (the original use case) uses Kafka as the central nervous system: every service emits events to Kafka, and downstream consumers (Hadoop ingestion, real-time analytics, monitoring, replication to other datacenters) read independently. The "log" abstraction lets LinkedIn add a new consumer (e.g., a new fraud-detection service) without touching producers — the new consumer reads from the beginning of the topic and catches up. **Netflix** uses Kafka for the playback pipeline: every play, pause, seek, and error is an event in a Kafka topic, consumed by real-time recommendations (sub-second lag), batch analytics (hours lag), and billing (minutes lag) — three independent consumer groups reading the same topic at different speeds. **Uber** uses Kafka for trip events: each trip's lifecycle (request, accept, start, end, payment) flows through Kafka, consumed by the pricing engine, the driver app, the rider app, and the analytics warehouse. **Instagram** uses Kafka for the notification fan-out: a like or comment is published to Kafka, and consumer groups fan out to push notifications, update feeds, and trigger analytics. The common pattern is "many consumers, one stream, replay-on-demand" — Kafka's killer feature.

The operational considerations are non-trivial. **Partition count** sets the parallelism ceiling: a topic with 12 partitions supports at most 12 consumers in a group (extra consumers are idle); adding partitions later is possible but breaks key-based ordering (a key hashed to partition 5 may hash to partition 17 after a re-partition). The rule is to over-provision partitions (start with 12–24, even if you need only 3 today) to avoid re-partitioning. **Retention** sets how long messages are kept: `retention.ms` (time-based, default 7 days) or `retention.bytes` (size-based, default -1 = unlimited); for replay use cases, set retention to 30+ days. **Consumer group rebalances** are the operational pain point: when a consumer joins or leaves, Kafka pauses consumption and reassigns partitions, causing a brief (seconds to minutes) stall — mitigated by static partition assignment (KIP-429) and incremental cooperative rebalancing (KIP-429). **Exactly-once** is supported via the transactional producer (`transactional.id` + two-phase commit between producer and consumer offset commit), but adds overhead and is opt-in; the default is at-least-once, requiring idempotent consumers. **Monitoring** focuses on consumer lag (the gap between the latest offset and the consumer's committed offset) — lag growing means the consumer cannot keep up, and alerting on lag is the single most important Kafka operational metric. The architect's rule: Kafka is the right choice for high-throughput streaming with replay and multi-consumer fan-out; it is over-engineering for a 100 msgs/sec notification pipeline that needs priorities and per-message delays — use RabbitMQ or SQS for that.

reads P2] end P1 -->|produce, key=K1 -> P0| B1 P2 -->|produce, key=K2 -> P1| B2 B1 -.->|replicate| B1r B2 -.->|replicate| B2r B3 -.->|replicate| B3r B1 -->|fetch from offset| C1 B2 --> C2 B3 --> C3 B1 --> CB1 B2 --> CB1 B3 --> CB2 ``` ### ASCII Diagram ``` +------+ produce(topic, key, msg) +----------------------------------+ |Prod |--------------------------------->| Topic: orders (3 partitions) | +------+ +----+--------+--------+-----------+ | | | partition 0 | | partition 1 | partition 2 +--------------+ +-------------+----------+ | [msg0, msg1, msg2..] | [msg0,msg1..] | [msg0..] v v v +------+ +------+ +------+ |Broker| |Broker| |Broker| | 1 | | 2 | | 3 | |(P0 L)| |(P1 L)| |(P2 L)| +--+---+ +--+---+ +--+---+ | | | replicate replicate replicate v v v +------+ +------+ +------+ |B2(P0 | |B3(P1 | |B1(P2 | | ISR) | | ISR) | | ISR) | +------+ +------+ +------+ Consumer Group A (3 consumers, 1 partition each): +----------+ fetch(P0, offset=42) +------+ |Consumer 1|<------------------------|B1 P0 | +----------+ +------+ Consumer Group B (2 consumers, 2+1 partitions, independent offset): +----------+ fetch(P0, offset=10) +------+ |Consumer |<------------------------|B1 P0 | | B1 |<------------------------|B2 P1 | +----------+ +------+ multi-consumer, replay-from-offset, durable retention = Kafka's killer feature ``` ### Walkthrough 1. Producers write messages to a topic, with an optional key. Kafka hashes the key to choose a partition (key=null means round-robin), so all messages with the same key land in the same partition in order. The producer batches messages (16KB or 5ms) and sends them to the partition's leader broker with `acks=all`, which writes to its log and waits for all ISR followers to replicate before acking the producer. 2. Each partition's leader broker serves reads: consumers in a group fetch batches of messages from their assigned partition's leader, starting at their last committed offset. The broker returns messages and the latest offset; the consumer processes them and commits its new offset back to Kafka (or to ZooKeeper in older versions). 3. If a consumer in a group dies, Kafka triggers a rebalance: the dead consumer's partitions are reassigned to surviving consumers, which resume from the last committed offset. Different consumer groups read the same topic independently at their own pace — Group A might be 5 seconds behind, Group B might be 5 hours behind, and Kafka serves both without conflict.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
**What this code covers**

- Toy Kafka-like broker: topic with partitions, key-based routing, consumer groups with offset tracking, leader + ISR replication sketch.
- Append-only log for one partition.
- A topic is N partitions; key hashed to pick a partition.
- A group of consumers sharing a topic.
- Leader + ISR assignment (simplified: leader is broker p%nb, ISR next rf-1)
- (in real Kafka, leader replicates to ISR followers here)
- Consumer group A: 3 consumers, each gets 1 partition
- Consumer group B: 2 consumers, partitions split 2+1, INDEPENDENT offsets

**Defines:** `Message`, `Partition`, `Topic`, `ConsumerGroup`

```python
"""
Toy Kafka-like broker: topic with partitions, key-based routing,
consumer groups with offset tracking, leader + ISR replication sketch.
"""
import hashlib, threading, time
from collections import defaultdict
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

@dataclass
class Message:
    offset: int
    key: str
    value: str

class Partition:
    """Append-only log for one partition. In real Kafka this is a file on disk."""
    def __init__(self, topic, idx):
        self.topic = topic; self.idx = idx
        self.log: list[Message] = []           # offset -> Message
        self.lock = threading.Lock()
    def append(self, key, value):
        with self.lock:
            offset = len(self.log)
            self.log.append(Message(offset, key, value))
            return offset
    def read(self, from_offset, max_msgs=100):
        return self.log[from_offset: from_offset + max_msgs]
    def latest_offset(self): return len(self.log)

class Topic:
    """A topic is N partitions; key hashed to pick a partition."""
    def __init__(self, name, n_partitions=3, replication_factor=3):
        self.name = name
        self.n_partitions = n_partitions
        self.rf = replication_factor
        self.partitions = [Partition(name, i) for i in range(n_partitions)]
        # leader + ISR assignment (simplified: leader is broker p%nb, ISR next rf-1)
        self.leaders = {p: (p % 3) for p in range(n_partitions)}
        self.isr = {p: [(p + i) % 3 for i in range(replication_factor)]
                    for p in range(n_partitions)}
    def _partition_for_key(self, key):
        if key is None: return hash(time.time()) % self.n_partitions  # round-robin
        return int(hashlib.md5(key.encode()).hexdigest(), 16) % self.n_partitions
    def produce(self, key, value):
        p = self._partition_for_key(key)
        off = self.partitions[p].append(key, value)
        # (in real Kafka, leader replicates to ISR followers here)
        return p, off

class ConsumerGroup:
    """A group of consumers sharing a topic. Each partition -> one consumer.
    Offsets are committed per (group, partition) and survive rebalances."""
    def __init__(self, name, topic):
        self.name = name; self.topic = topic
        self.offsets: dict[int, int] = defaultdict(int)  # partition -> next offset
        self.assignments: dict[int, str] = {}            # partition -> consumer_id
    def rebalance(self, consumer_ids: list[str]):
        """Assign each partition to exactly one consumer (round-robin)."""
        self.assignments = {}
        for p in range(self.topic.n_partitions):
            self.assignments[p] = consumer_ids[p % len(consumer_ids)]
    def poll(self, consumer_id, max_msgs=10):
        """Consumer fetches messages from its assigned partitions."""
        out = []
        for p, cid in self.assignments.items():
            if cid != consumer_id: continue
            msgs = self.topic.partitions[p].read(self.offsets[p], max_msgs)
            out.extend((p, m) for m in msgs)
            self.offsets[p] += len(msgs)
        return out
    def commit_offset(self, partition, offset):
        self.offsets[partition] = offset

# --- Demo ---
topic = Topic("orders", n_partitions=3, replication_factor=3)

# Producers
for i in range(9):
    key = f"user_{i % 3}"   # 3 users -> hash to 3 partitions, per-user ordering
    topic.produce(key, f"order_{i}")

print("Partition sizes:", [p.latest_offset() for p in topic.partitions])

# Consumer group A: 3 consumers, each gets 1 partition
groupA = ConsumerGroup("analytics", topic)
groupA.rebalance(["c1", "c2", "c3"])
for cid in ["c1", "c2", "c3"]:
    msgs = groupA.poll(cid)
    for p, m in msgs:
        print(f"  groupA/{cid} <- P{p} off={m.offset} key={m.key} val={m.value}")

# Consumer group B: 2 consumers, partitions split 2+1, INDEPENDENT offsets
groupB = ConsumerGroup("audit", topic)
groupB.rebalance(["b1", "b2"])
for cid in ["b1", "b2"]:
    msgs = groupB.poll(cid)
    print(f"  groupB/{cid} read {len(msgs)} msgs (independent of groupA)")

# Replay: reset groupB's offsets to 0 and read from the beginning
for p in range(topic.n_partitions):
    groupB.commit_offset(p, 0)
print("groupB replaying from offset 0...")
for cid in ["b1", "b2"]:
    msgs = groupB.poll(cid)
    print(f"  groupB/{cid} re-read {len(msgs)} msgs (Kafka allows replay)")
```
